tips.text: Judge a suit while standing relaxed, not while holding your breath or striking a pose.
tips.why: Only your natural posture shows how it really fits.

tips.text: Buy a jacket for its shoulders first: the seam should land where your shoulder ends.
tips.why: Shoulders are the hardest part to alter; most other areas can be adjusted.

tips.text: Treat dimples at the top of the sleeve as a warning sign of a poor shoulder fit or a cut that doesn't suit your posture.
tips.why: They rarely disappear and spoil the shoulder line.

tips.text: Lapels should lie flat against the chest without gaping or lifting.
tips.why: Gaping lapels make even a costly suit look cheap.

tips.text: The jacket should button without pulling, leaving room to slide a flat hand inside.
tips.why: Too tight causes strain lines; too loose looks sloppy.

tips.text: Look for gentle waist shaping in a jacket, neither clinging at the button nor hanging straight like a box.
tips.why: Shaping suggests your build without exaggerating it.

tips.text: The jacket should cover your seat, with the hem around mid-palm when your arms hang at your sides.
tips.why: Too short looks juvenile, too long looks awkward.

tips.text: Jacket sleeves should end at the wrist bone, showing roughly a quarter to half an inch of shirt cuff.
tips.why: The cuff visually separates jacket from hand and looks finished.

tips.text: The jacket collar should sit flush on the shirt collar with no gap at the back of the neck.
tips.why: A gap there signals poor fit.

tips.text: Read the jacket's back: horizontal creases mean too tight, vertical folds mean excess cloth, and spreading vents mean tight hips or seat.
tips.why: The back exposes fit problems that are hard to hide.

tips.text: Test a suit by reaching, walking and sitting; it should settle back into place without constant tugging.
tips.why: A suit that fights your movements doesn't fit.

tips.text: Suit trousers should stay up without a belt doing the work, feel comfortable seated and standing, and not sag at the seat.
tips.why: Well-fitting trousers hold their shape on their own.

tips.text: Leave room to move in the thigh, but avoid both excess fabric and cling around thigh and knee.
tips.why: Trousers should move easily without looking baggy or tight.

tips.text: A slight break is the safest trouser length; avoid fabric pooling on the shoe, and the back hem shouldn't catch the heel.
tips.why: Break length shapes the whole line of the leg.

tips.text: Check the jacket unbuttoned as well; it should still look sharp worn open.
tips.why: Most men wear their jacket open much of the time.

tips.text: Choose the size that fits shoulders, chest and seat, then have the waist, sleeves and trouser length tailored.
tips.why: Structural changes are costly and rarely succeed, and making a suit smaller is easier than larger.

tips.text: Avoid jackets cut too short or too tight and trousers whose waist sits too low.
tips.why: These common mistakes make a suit look juvenile or sloppy.
